stories.headline: Trump Nominates Lance Schroyer as First Senate-Confirmed ICE Director in Nearly a Decade
stories.summary:
President Trump announced Saturday he will nominate Lance Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper and U.S. Marine with 29 years of law enforcement experience, to serve as director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Schroyer currently serves as an adviser to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and previously led deportation operations in Oklahoma under an ICE-partnered program. Trump praised him on Truth Social as a "PATRIOT with real operational experience."

The nomination is notable because ICE has not had a Senate-confirmed director since the Obama administration — a gap of nearly a decade. The position most recently became vacant when former acting director Todd Lyons resigned at the end of May; David Venturella, a former private prison executive, had been serving in an interim capacity since then.

Schroyer's nomination comes as ICE sits at the center of the administration's aggressive immigration enforcement agenda, making Senate confirmation of a permanent director a significant political and operational milestone. Supporters argue a confirmed director will bring stability and credibility to the agency's leadership during a period of high-tempo enforcement operations. Critics, including immigration advocates and some Democratic lawmakers, have raised concerns about the pace and methods of ICE deportation campaigns and are expected to scrutinize Schroyer's record during confirmation hearings.

The nomination was covered by 12 outlets across the political spectrum, reflecting its broad significance to the ongoing national debate over immigration enforcement.

stories.headline: Serbia's Vucic Announces Imminent Resignation to Seek Prime Ministership Amid Protest Pressure
stories.summary:
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic announced Saturday that he will resign from the presidency within weeks, a move designed to position himself to lead his ruling party into early parliamentary elections expected later this year. Vucic said stepping down from the presidency would allow him to campaign as the party's leader and, if the party wins, return to power as prime minister — effectively trading one office for another while retaining political dominance.

The announcement comes after months of sustained anti-government protests in Serbia that have put significant pressure on Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party. Demonstrators have demanded greater democratic accountability, media freedom, and an end to what critics describe as a decade of consolidated one-party rule. The protests were among the largest in the country's post-communist history.

Vucic's maneuver reflects a calculated political gamble: by stepping down from a largely ceremonial presidential role and entering the parliamentary arena directly, he aims to energize his base and reclaim the political offensive ahead of elections. Opponents argue the move is a transparent attempt to reset the political clock and circumvent growing public opposition without making substantive policy concessions.

The development carries implications for Serbia's relationship with the European Union, which has been closely watching Belgrade's democratic backsliding, as well as its fraught relations with Kosovo and its position between Western partners and Russia.

stories.headline: Australia to Expand Enforcement Powers for World-First Under-16 Social Media Ban
stories.summary:
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced Saturday that the government will grant its online safety regulator significantly expanded enforcement powers and raise maximum penalties for violations of its landmark law banning children under 16 from using social media platforms. Albanese said major technology companies are not doing enough to ensure compliance, and that current enforcement tools are insufficient to compel cooperation.

Australia became the first country in the world to enact such a ban when the legislation passed in late 2024, requiring platforms to verify users' ages and remove underage accounts. The government says platforms have continued to allow children to bypass the restrictions through inadequate age-verification systems, prompting the need for stronger regulatory teeth.

The move intensifies what has become a global flashpoint between governments and large technology companies over child safety online. Supporters of the ban argue that social media poses documented mental health risks to minors and that voluntary industry measures have repeatedly proven inadequate. The tech industry and some civil liberties groups have pushed back, arguing that age verification systems raise serious privacy concerns and that determined minors will find workarounds regardless.

The Australian model is being closely watched by legislators in the United States, the United Kingdom, and the European Union as a potential template for similar regulations, making this enforcement escalation a significant data point in the international policy debate.

stories.headline: Trump Unveils Limited-Edition Passport Featuring His Own Photo, First for a Sitting President
stories.summary:
The Trump administration has released a commemorative limited-edition U.S. passport featuring a photograph of President Trump seated at the Resolute Desk alongside the Declaration of Independence, with his signature below the image. The State Department said the passports will be available beginning July 6, only while supplies last, and only through in-person appointments at the Washington Passport Agency or designated special events. It marks the first time a sitting president has appeared on a U.S. passport.

The release is timed to coincide with the nation's 250th anniversary celebrations this summer. Trump described the document on Truth Social as the "U.S.A.'s New Passport" and the White House dubbed it a "patriot passport." The design was first announced in April in a slightly different form; the final version includes the "250" anniversary marker. Standard U.S. passports currently depict historical scenes and American symbols.

The passport is the latest in a series of moves by the Trump administration to affix the president's name or likeness to American institutions and official documents. Trump is also set to become the first sitting president with his signature on U.S. banknotes, and the U.S. Mint has announced a commemorative gold coin featuring his image. An earlier plan to add Trump's name to the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts was later reversed.

The move has drawn both enthusiastic support from backers who see it as a fitting patriotic gesture and criticism from those who argue it inappropriately conflates the presidency with national identity. It is not yet clear whether citizens applying for passports at the Washington agency will be able to opt out of the commemorative design.

stories.headline: Millions Dropped ACA Coverage After Enhanced Subsidies Expired
stories.summary:
Approximately four million Americans dropped Affordable Care Act health insurance plans this year after enhanced subsidies expired, according to new data released Friday by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. The figures represent the most comprehensive accounting to date of the enrollment fallout following Congress's failure to extend the enhanced subsidies, which had been in place since the COVID-19 pandemic era.

With the subsidies gone, many enrollees faced double- or even triple-digit percentage increases in their monthly premium payments, pricing them out of coverage. The CMS data release comes as congressional Republicans and the White House continue to debate the future of ACA funding and Medicaid in broader budget negotiations.

Supporters of the ACA argue the enrollment collapse demonstrates the critical role federal subsidies play in making insurance accessible to lower- and middle-income Americans, and are calling for their restoration. Critics on the right contend the subsidy structure was an unsustainable expansion of federal spending and that market-based alternatives can better serve consumers over the long term.

The loss of coverage for four million people raises significant public health concerns, as uninsured individuals are less likely to seek preventive care and more likely to rely on emergency services. Health policy analysts say the figures will likely intensify debate over subsidy renewal ahead of the midterm elections.

stories.headline: Utah's Cottonwood Fire Grows to 144 Square Miles, Largest Active Blaze in U.S., Forcing New Evacuations
stories.summary:
A fast-moving wildfire in southern Utah, the Cottonwood Fire, expanded overnight to more than 144 square miles, making it the largest active wildfire currently burning in the United States. Driven by gusts reaching 45 miles per hour and humidity levels in the single digits, the blaze forced additional evacuations across multiple communities and grounded air tankers and helicopters that crews depend on for aerial suppression.

The fire severely damaged the Eagle Point ski resort in Beaver County and forced closures of campgrounds in Fishlake National Forest. In the town of Marysvale, ash rained from skies darkened by smoke, and officials issued air quality warnings across a wide area. Two other fires in the region — the Iron and Cherry fires — merged overnight, together covering roughly 91 square miles and standing at 38 percent containment.

A state meteorologist warned residents at a community meeting that Utah faces a full 48 hours of critical fire weather not seen in the state in five years. Utah state officials noted that Salt Lake City recorded its warmest winter on record earlier this year, with temperatures nearly 8 degrees above normal, contributing to the exceptionally dry conditions fueling the fires.

No fatalities or injuries have been reported so far. Smoke from the Cottonwood Fire was visible as far away as Colorado, though air quality at major tourist destinations such as Zion and Bryce Canyon national parks remained largely unaffected beyond some haze.

stories.headline: California Reaches $351.7 Billion Budget Deal Including New Software Sales Tax
stories.summary:
California Governor Gavin Newsom and top Democratic legislative leaders have reached agreement on a $351.7 billion state budget that includes a newly proposed tax on digital software sales. The deal represents one of the largest state budgets in U.S. history and comes as California works to close a significant fiscal gap.

The budget agreement arrives amid a broader political moment for Newsom, who separately called this week for a national "billionaires' tax" on the ultra-wealthy — a proposal that drew attention partly because it came just as a state-level wealth tax measure he opposes qualified for California's November ballot. Critics, including from the right, characterized the national proposal as political opportunism ahead of a widely expected 2028 presidential run.

The software sales tax component of the budget is a novel approach to broadening California's revenue base as the state's economy becomes increasingly digital. Business groups have raised concerns that taxing software transactions could harm the technology sector, a cornerstone of California's economy, while budget supporters argue it ensures digital commerce pays into public services at rates comparable to physical goods.

The budget deal is seen as a significant legislative milestone given the scale of California's fiscal challenges, though it will face scrutiny over whether the new revenue measures are sufficient to sustain long-term spending commitments. The state's decisions often signal broader policy trends that other states and the federal government eventually follow.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Strikes Iran Again After Ceasefire Violation; Iran Attacks Bahrain as Strait of Hormuz Crisis Deepens
stories.summary:
The United States military conducted retaliatory strikes against Iranian missile and drone storage sites and coastal radar locations on Friday, hours after Iran attacked a Singapore-flagged cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday. President Trump called the drone strike a "foolish violation" of the memorandum of understanding signed last week declaring an end to the U.S.-Iran war. U.S. Central Command said the strikes concluded after approximately 90 minutes.

Iran responded by launching a drone attack against Bahrain early Saturday, targeting the Gulf state that hosts the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet. Bahrain condemned the strikes as a "blatant violation" of its sovereignty. Iran said its retaliatory actions were conducted under Article 51 of the UN Charter, citing the right to self-defense, and accused the U.S. of violating the ceasefire deal first.

The escalating exchanges have cast serious doubt over the durability of the peace agreement, which was signed just one week ago. Analysts say the deal is at risk of collapse, with the core dispute centering on differing interpretations of the MOU's provisions governing ship passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Vice President Vance said Friday that Iran "signed a ceasefire agreement" and that if Tehran had disagreements about how the MOU was being applied, it should "pick up the phone."

Separately on Friday, the U.S., Israel, and Lebanon announced a trilateral framework agreement aimed at eventually ending Israel's occupation of southern Lebanon and reducing Iranian influence in the country through its support of Hezbollah. However, Hezbollah chief Hassan Nasrallah called the deal "null and void," raising significant questions about whether the agreement can lead to lasting peace.

stories.headline: Burkina Faso Severs Diplomatic Ties with France, Accusing Paris of Neo-Colonial Ambitions
stories.summary:
Burkina Faso's military junta formally severed diplomatic ties with France on Friday, with communications minister Pingdwendé Gilbert Ouédraogo accusing Paris of "ceaseless activism" against the country and "neo-colonial ambitions." The French foreign ministry called the decision "hostile and unfounded" and urged French nationals in the country to exercise "heightened vigilance."

Relations between the two countries have deteriorated sharply since Captain Ibrahim Traoré seized power in a coup in 2022 and pursued anti-Western policies, including expelling French troops that had been fighting alongside Burkinabe forces against an Islamist insurgency. The junta has since pivoted toward China and Russia.

The break marks the latest rupture between France and its former colonies in the Sahel region. Burkina Faso's neighbors Mali and Niger have followed similar trajectories, and in January 2025 the three countries formally broke away from the West African regional bloc ECOWAS to form the Alliance of Sahel States. France has had no ambassador in Burkina Faso since January 2023, and Ouagadougou expelled three French diplomats in 2024 on charges of subversive activities that Paris denied.

The junta's statement specified that the severance applied to the "institutional framework of relations" and did not affect historical, cultural, and social ties between the two peoples. The decision nonetheless represents a significant reshaping of West Africa's post-colonial security and diplomatic architecture, with broad implications for France's remaining influence across the continent.

stories.headline: Andy Burnham Poised to Become UK Prime Minister, Faces Economic Constraints Despite Popular Mandate
stories.summary:
Andy Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, was sworn into Parliament on Friday and is on course to become Britain's next prime minister after Keir Starmer's resignation Monday. Burnham is currently the sole contestant for the Labour Party leadership and is expected to take office on July 17 if no other candidates enter the race. His ascension would make him the seventh prime minister in a decade.

Burnham is widely regarded as sitting to the left of Starmer within the Labour Party and has built a reputation for popular, hands-on governance during a decade leading Greater Manchester, a region that experienced significant economic revival under his tenure. However, political analysts warn he will be constrained by the platform Labour was elected on in 2024 and has pledged to revive the economy without exceeding current government spending and borrowing plans — a commitment aimed at reassuring markets still nervous following the 2022 Liz Truss fiscal crisis.

His main challenges will be overcoming Starmer's failure to deliver promised economic growth, repairing public services, and addressing the cost of living. He is expected to lay out his economic vision in a speech next week.

"At the moment, Andy Burnham is being almost hailed and held up as a folk hero that will save British politics," said Matthew Flinders, politics professor at the University of Sheffield. "The tide is changing and the big issue for Andy Burnham is that when the world suddenly moves against him and he becomes a folk devil, will he sustain the pressure?"

stories.headline: DR Congo Files ICJ Case Against Rwanda Over Decades of Cross-Border Conflict
stories.summary:
The Democratic Republic of Congo filed a case against Rwanda at the International Court of Justice on Friday, accusing its neighbor of violating multiple international treaties by dispatching forces and backing armed groups to carry out unlawful military operations on Congolese territory. Congolese Justice Minister Guillaume Andali said his country is seeking accountability for alleged breaches of conventions covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights, and torture.

Rwanda has not yet responded to the filing but has long dismissed evidence that it supports the M23 rebel group, which captured large parts of the mineral-rich eastern DRC, including the regional capital Goma, in January. UN experts and Western governments have stated that Rwanda backs M23. The fighting has continued despite a U.S.-brokered peace deal signed in December.

The roots of the conflict trace back to the 1994 Rwandan genocide, after which an estimated one million Hutus fled into what is now DR Congo, stoking ethnic tensions that have fueled successive armed conflicts and foreign interventions for over three decades. This is DR Congo's third attempt to bring Rwanda before the ICJ; previous cases were dropped or dismissed on jurisdictional grounds. The ICJ will now examine the claims and consider Congo's request that Rwanda cease alleged crimes and pay reparations.

stories.headline: Update: Republican Ohio Governor Calls Supreme Court TPS Ruling 'A Mistake' as State Faces Haitian Migrant Uncertainty
stories.summary:
Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, a Republican, publicly criticized the Supreme Court's Thursday ruling in Mullin v. Doe, which cleared the way for the Trump administration to end Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and Syrians residing in the United States. DeWine, whose state is home to more than 10,000 Haitian migrants — many in the Dayton and Columbus areas — called the decision a policy mistake, even while acknowledging it as a legal ruling.

The governor's dissent from his own party's position illustrates the practical tensions the ruling creates for Republican-led states that have absorbed large immigrant communities over recent years. DeWine has previously argued that Haitian immigrants have contributed economically and culturally to Ohio communities that were facing population decline.

The ruling represents one of the Trump administration's most significant immigration victories, with the Supreme Court also separately allowing border turnback policies. Supporters of the TPS terminations argue the protections were meant to be temporary and that their extension has become indefinite, incentivizing illegal immigration. Critics, including immigrant advocacy groups and some local officials, warn the decision could separate families and destabilize communities that have come to depend on these workers.

stories.headline: Trump-Meloni Alliance Fractures Further After Trump Claims Italian PM 'Begged' for Photo
stories.summary:
The once-celebrated political alliance between U.S. President Donald Trump and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has deteriorated sharply following a series of public confrontations over the past several months. What began as one of the most closely watched partnerships in Western politics — Meloni held a front-row seat at Trump's January 2025 inauguration and later served as a key EU interlocutor during tariff negotiations — has fractured over Italy's refusal to allow U.S. military aircraft to use a NATO airbase in Sicily and Meloni's public rebuke of Trump's attack on Pope Leo XIV.

The latest rupture came after the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains in France, where officials from both sides described a productive meeting and reduced tensions. Within days, Trump told an Italian broadcaster that Meloni had "begged" him for a photograph at the summit, saying he "felt sorry for her" — comments that were aired in Italy but never released in English. Meloni responded publicly and sharply.

The falling-out carries significant diplomatic weight. Meloni had positioned her closeness to Trump as evidence of her credibility on the international stage and as leverage in managing EU-U.S. relations on tariffs and other issues. Analysts note that Trump's unpredictability has repeatedly undermined European leaders who sought to cultivate personal ties with him. Italy is a NATO member and a major economy, and the relationship's deterioration complicates transatlantic coordination at a sensitive moment.

stories.headline: Update: Venezuela Earthquake Death Toll Reaches 920 as Families Search Rubble Without Government Aid
stories.summary:
The death toll from Venezuela's back-to-back 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes has climbed to at least 920, with more than 51,000 people reported missing nearly two days after the disaster struck. Citizens in the hardest-hit areas, particularly La Guaira just north of Caracas, have taken search and rescue operations into their own hands, reporting a near-absence of government rescue teams despite official statements projecting a robust state response.

Families used hammers and power tools to cut through collapsed concrete slabs in search of buried relatives, as aid agencies warned that the critical 48-to-72-hour window for finding survivors alive was closing. Venezuelan authorities announced Friday night they would block access to La Guaira without official permits, citing chaos and traffic hampering search efforts — a move that drew alarm from residents already frustrated by inadequate help.

Acting President Delcy Rodríguez, who assumed leadership after the disaster, said the government was mounting a full response and welcomed international aid. Dozens of rescue teams from around the world have arrived or are en route. The disaster presents an enormous governance challenge for Venezuela, which was already facing a severe humanitarian and political crisis before the quakes struck.

stories.headline: U.S. Government Lifts Export Restrictions on Anthropic's Most Advanced AI Model
stories.summary:
The U.S. government has lifted its export ban on Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5, its most powerful artificial intelligence model, allowing the company to share it with more than 100 select companies and partners. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick confirmed the decision in a letter to Anthropic, with the company stating the restrictions had been resolved after the Trump administration reviewed concerns about the technology's potential national security implications.

Separately, OpenAI announced Friday it will preview its newest GPT-5.6 model series — including variants named Sol, Terra, and Luna — with a select group of partners before a broader public rollout, also at the behest of the U.S. government. The coordinated approach signals a new framework in which Washington is actively managing the release cadence of frontier AI systems before they reach the wider market.

The moves represent a significant shift in federal AI policy, with the government playing a gatekeeper role for the most capable commercial AI models. The decisions follow months of tension between AI developers and regulators over dual-use risks, and come as the U.S. seeks to maintain competitive dominance over China in advanced AI development.

stories.headline: Trump Religious Liberty Commission Report Calls for 'Building Bridges' Between Church and State
stories.summary:
A draft final report from President Trump's Religious Liberty Commission, released Friday, calls for "building bridges between church and state" — language that represents a direct departure from the longstanding American legal doctrine of church-state separation rooted in the First Amendment's Establishment Clause. The report states that "Americans must know their rights and stand with courage when those rights are challenged."

The commission's framing signals a continued push by the Trump administration to expand the role of religion in public life and government, building on prior executive actions including support for faith-based organizations receiving federal funding and the promotion of religious exemptions from federal regulations. Supporters argue the shift corrects what they see as decades of government hostility toward religious expression in the public square.

Critics, including civil liberties groups and many constitutional scholars, contend that replacing separation with a "bridges" framework risks eroding protections against government establishment of religion and could disadvantage non-Christian or non-religious Americans. The report's recommendations are expected to inform future executive actions and potential legislative proposals on religious liberty.

stories.headline: Newsom Calls for National 'Billionaires' Tax' While Opposing Similar Measure in California
stories.summary:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom, widely seen as a prospective 2028 presidential candidate, published a sweeping economic agenda Friday calling for a national minimum tax on individuals with a net worth above $100 million, new restrictions on borrowing against stock portfolios to avoid taxes, revised inheritance tax rules, and a restoration of corporate tax rates to pre-Trump levels. He also proposed a national public equity fund that would give every American a stake in artificial intelligence companies, arguing that AI-driven wealth concentration threatens democracy.

The announcement came one day after a major California health care union pledged to advance a state ballot measure imposing a one-time 5% tax on the assets of California-based billionaires — a measure Newsom opposes. He argues that taxing wealth at the state level is ineffective because billionaires can relocate to lower-tax states, and that the problem requires a federal solution. California, home to more billionaires than any other state, has seen repeated debates over whether high taxes drive out wealthy residents.

Newsom's proposals align him with the Democratic Party's populist left and mark a clear positioning ahead of a potential presidential run. Conservatives have pointed to the contradiction of Newsom championing higher taxes nationally while blocking them in his own state, arguing it reflects political opportunism rather than coherent policy. Supporters counter that his logic — that only federal action can prevent billionaires from tax-shopping between states — is economically sound.
